summary: Clarifies how the SIP REFER method is affected by the revised event framework in RFC 6665. It points out the consequences of the changed requirements and updates the REFER definition in RFC 3515 to remove ambiguity.

plainLanguage.summary: When the rulebook for one game changes, a neighboring game's rules need a note too. This is that note for call transfers.

subtitle: Spells out how SIP call-transfer REFER requests must change now that the SIP event framework requires GRUUs.

tldr.problem: RFC 6665 revised the SIP event notification framework, but a REFER request creates an implicit subscription, so its rules for GRUUs, dialogs and response codes needed clarifying.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC requires a GRUU in the Contact of a UA accepting a subscription-creating REFER, requires such a REFER to be sent out of dialog, and replaces the 202 response with 200.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 3515 so that REFER matches RFC 6665 and avoids a problematic extra dialog usage inside an existing dialog.

today: RFC 7647 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3515, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why REFER Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
The SIP REFER method relies on the SIP-Specific Event Notification framework, which RFC 6665 revised. This document highlights what the changed requirements mean for REFER and updates RFC 3515 to remove ambiguity.

Accepting a REFER without extensions creates an implicit SIP-Events subscription. If the REFER was sent inside an existing dialog, that subscription creates a new, problematic dialog usage within it (see RFC 5057). The norefersub extension from RFC 4488 asks to suppress the subscription but cannot prevent it.

Some specialized environments, such as 3GPP, use out-of-signaling agreements to avoid the extra subscription, but that does not help when interoperating with implementations that lack the mechanism. The extensions in RFC 7614 give a standard way to avoid any additional dialog usage.
sections.plainLanguage: Passing a call to someone else quietly starts a second conversation inside the first one, which causes confusion. This note explains how to avoid the mix-up.

sections.title: GRUU Use Is Mandatory
sections.content:
Section 4.5.1 of RFC 6665 makes a GRUU (RFC 5627) mandatory for notifiers to implement and use as the local target of the subscription a REFER creates. So a user agent (UA) accepting a REFER that creates a subscription MUST populate its Contact header field with a GRUU.

A UA that might become a notifier, for example by accepting such a REFER, needs to include a GRUU in the Contact of dialog-forming and target-refresh methods such as INVITE. That way out-of-dialog REFER requests for any resulting INVITE dialog reach this UA. Extensions such as RFC 7614 can relax this by defining a REFER that cannot create an implicit subscription.
sections.plainLanguage: A GRUU is like a direct phone number that always reaches you personally. If you might take a call transfer, you must give out that number.

sections.title: Dialog Reuse Is Prohibited
sections.content:
If the other side of an existing dialog gave a GRUU as its Contact, sending a REFER that might add a dialog usage inside that dialog is prohibited. A UA building a REFER that could create an implicit subscription MUST send it as an out-of-dialog request per RFC 3261, so it has no tag parameter in its To header field. The exception is an older RFC 3515 implementation that has not been updated for RFC 6665, recognised by the absence of a GRUU in the remote target.

Using the norefersub option tag does not change this, even in a Require header field, because the recipient may still reply with a Refer-Sub header of true and create the subscription.

To point at an existing dialog, such as for call transfer in RFC 5589, a UA MUST use the Target-Dialog extension from RFC 4538, and UAs accepting REFER must be able to process it. If a UA can be certain no implicit subscription will result, for example by requiring an extension like RFC 7614, it MAY send the REFER inside an existing dialog.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not start the transfer chat inside the call that is already going. Send it separately and just say which call you mean, unless you are sure it will not cause a mix-up.

sections.title: The 202 Response Code Is Deprecated
sections.content:
Section 8.3.1 of RFC 6665 requires that elements not send a 202 response to a SUBSCRIBE request but use 200 instead, and that any 202 received be treated as a 200. The RFC applies the same change to REFER.

An element accepting a REFER MUST NOT reply with 202 and MUST treat any 202 it receives as identical to 200. Wherever RFC 3515 requires a 202, a 200 must be sent instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Where people used to answer with one kind of okay, they must now use the ordinary okay, and treat the old one as the same thing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC introduces no new security considerations directly. The updated considerations in RFC 6665 apply to the implicit subscription created by an accepted REFER request.
sections.plainLanguage: This note adds no new safety rules. The safety rules from the main rulebook still cover the extra subscription.
